Heed
heed
n. and v. (careful attention, watchful regard; rendering Hebrew shamar, Greek blepo and prosecho)
From the Saxon hedan, to observe, to guard, to care for. The old sense is custodial rather than merely mental — to take heed of a thing is to keep watch over it, which is why the Hebrew behind it is often shamar, the verb used of keeping a garden and keeping a commandment.

Biblical Definition

To take heed is to keep watch, and the Bible directs it at four objects in particular. First, at one's own way, with the word as the standard: “Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word” (Psalm 119:9). Note the two halves — heed alone is mere carefulness; heed according to thy word is sanctification, because it measures the way against something outside the self. Second, at the danger of self-confidence: “let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). The warning is aimed precisely at the man who feels no need of it, which is why it is placed after the wilderness examples; those who fell in the desert had all seen the sea divided. Third, at the truth already heard, lest it drift: “we ought to give the more earnest heed to the things which we have heard, lest at any time we should let them slip” (Hebrews 2:1). The image is nautical — a vessel carried past the harbour by an unnoticed current. Apostasy is rarely a decision; it is usually a drift. Fourth, at the minister's own soul and message together: “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine” (1 Timothy 4:16). Paul will not let the two be separated, and the order is significant.

Webster 1828 Definition

Careful attention; watchful regard. Scripture points it at one's way measured by the word, at the self-confidence that precedes a fall, at truth that slips by drift, and at the minister's life and doctrine together.

expand to see more

HEED, v.t. [Sax. hedan, to observe, to take care.] To mind; to regard with care; to take notice of; to attend to.

2. HEED, n. Care; attention; notice; observation; regard; often with take.

3. Caution; watchfulness against danger; as, to take heed of a snare.

4. Seriousness; a state of being earnest or attentive.

5. In Scripture, to take heed is often to beware, to guard the soul; take heed lest ye fall.

Key Scripture

Psalm 119:9 — "BETH. Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word."

1 Corinthians 10:12 — "Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall."

Hebrews 2:1 — "Therefore we ought to give the more earnest heed to the things which we have heard, lest at any time we should let them slip."

1 Timothy 4:16 — "Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee."

Modern Corruption

Vigilance over the soul is recast as morbid introspection or anxiety, and the warnings against falling are muted by an assurance that never examines itself.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors both disable this word. The first hears every take heed as a threat to assurance and answers it with a slogan — once saved, always saved — used to silence the very warnings God gave for the preserving of his people. But Scripture's warnings are among the ordinary means by which the elect persevere; a man kept by God is kept partly by heeding. Perseverance of the saints is not the claim that a professing man cannot fall away, but that a truly regenerate man will not, and one reason he will not is that the Spirit makes such warnings land. The second error treats self-examination as unhealthy inwardness, and the modern vocabulary of anxiety is used to excuse a soul from ever looking at itself. 1 Corinthians 10:12 is addressed to exactly the man who would rather not.

The principle to recover is that heed has an external standard. Psalm 119:9 does not say a young man cleanses his way by being careful; it says by taking heed according to thy word. Introspection with no rule outside the self is a maze with no exit, and it deserves the modern suspicion it gets. Examination against Scripture is a different act entirely: it has a fixed measure, it can reach a verdict, and it ends in either repentance or peace rather than in endless circling.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shamar is to keep, guard, watch over — the verb of keeping the garden and keeping the commandments. Greek blepo is to look at, and prosecho, to hold the mind toward.

expand to see more

Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, guard, observe; used of Eden, of the law, and of the soul.

Hebrew nashab / qashab (H7181) — to prick up the ears, to attend closely to what is said.

Greek blepo (G991) — to see, to look to; take heed lest he fall, 1 Corinthians 10:12.

Greek prosecho (G4337) — to hold the mind toward, to give attention; Hebrews 2:1.

Greek epecho (G1907) — to hold fast, to give heed; take heed unto thyself, 1 Timothy 4:16.

Usage

"Of the cleansing of a young man's way: by taking heed thereto according to thy word (Psalm 119:9)."

"Of the peril of confidence: let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall (1 Corinthians 10:12)."

"Of truth lost by drift: lest at any time we should let them slip (Hebrews 2:1)."
